claim: Adaptive Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Debate (A-HMAD) with specialized agent roles, dynamic routing, and learned consensus achieves 4-6% absolute accuracy gains over standard homogeneous multi-agent debate across six benchmarks.
stance_target: heterogeneous specialized-agent debate as an adversarial review architecture for an AI software factory
scope_conditions: six benchmarks: arithmetic QA, GSM8K, MMLU, factual biography generation, chess strategy, TruthfulQA (2025 study)
quoted_support: Notably, A-HMAD achieves 4-6% absolute accuracy gains over standard debate on these tasks, and reduces factual errors by over 30% in biography facts.

claim: A learned consensus mechanism that weights agent votes by reliability and argument confidence resolves agent disagreements more accurately than simple majority voting: 78% correct (39/50) versus 68% correct (34/50) on disputed GSM8K problems, a 31% relative error reduction.
stance_target: using simple majority voting as the consensus mechanism in multi-agent adversarial review pipelines
scope_conditions: 50 GSM8K problems with agent disagreement in the final debate round
quoted_support: Majority vote correctness: 68% (34/50 correct by simple majority). Learned consensus correctness: 78% (39/50 correct when using f_phi). Thus the learned consensus improved resolution of disagreements by reducing errors by ~31% relative.

claim: Role diversity matters more than raw agent count: removing a specialized fact-checking role ('Knowledge Guru') dropped accuracy 2.3-2.8%, merging two distinct roles into one hybrid dropped accuracy 3.5-4.1%, while duplicating a role (redundant agent) yielded under 0.5% gain.
stance_target: designing distinct specialized department-like agent roles rather than adding more identical agents in a software factory architecture
quoted_support: removing the Knowledge Guru decreased accuracy by 2.3-2.8%, while merging Solver and Checker caused a larger drop of 3.5-4.1%. Duplicating a role yielded minimal gains (<0.5%)... distinct and complementary roles are important for maintaining diversity and reasoning robustness.

claim: Accuracy gains from adding more debating agents and more debate rounds show strong diminishing returns: on Arithmetic, accuracy rises 72% (1 agent) to 87% (3) to 90% (5) to only 91% (7 agents); debate rounds show 75% (0 rounds) to 83% (1) to 87.5% (2) to 89% (3 rounds), with two rounds capturing most of the gain.
stance_target: cost/resource optimization pillar -- justifying capping agent/round counts rather than scaling indefinitely for marginal accuracy gains
quoted_support: Accuracy on Arithmetic: 1 agent 72%, 3 agents 87%, 5 agents 90%, 7 agents 91%. There are diminishing returns beyond 5 agents... 0 rounds... 75%, 1 round 83%, 2 rounds 87.5%, 3 rounds 89%. It appears two debate rounds capture most gains.

claim: Agent heterogeneity increased rather than decreased consensus convergence: A-HMAD reached unanimous agreement in 92% of arithmetic problems and 85% of GSM8K problems, compared to 88% and 80% respectively for the homogeneous debate baseline.
stance_target: the assumption that specialized/diverse agents will disagree more and slow consensus in multi-agent review systems
quoted_support: agents reached unanimous agreement in 92% of arithmetic problems and 85% of GSM8K problems, up from 88% and 80% respectively in the homogeneous debate baseline. This suggests heterogeneity did not reduce convergence; in fact it slightly increased it.

claim: Adding a skepticism-specialized agent to the debate reduced false answers by approximately 20% on TruthfulQA (a dataset designed to induce hallucinations) compared to a single LLM.
stance_target: zero-hallucination quality control via a dedicated skeptic/adversarial agent role
scope_conditions: TruthfulQA side experiment, small-scale, not in main results table, 2025
quoted_support: On TruthfulQA (a dataset of tricky questions designed to induce hallucinations), A-HMAD (with an added agent specialized in skepticism) reduced false answers by ~20% compared to single LLM.

claim: In a case study, a specialized Knowledge Guru agent corrected a fabricated fact (both Solver and Checker agents guessed a scientist's PhD year as 1980 with expressed uncertainty; the Guru recalled the correct year, 1978, which the Checker then verified and the consensus adopted).
stance_target: specialized fact-verification agent roles catching hallucinations that generalist agents would have missed
scope_conditions: single worked example from biography-QA case study, 2025
quoted_support: the Solver and Checker both guessed a plausible year (1980) but expressed uncertainty. The Guru agent, having been prompted to recall specifics, produced 'He earned his PhD in 1978.' ... Without the Guru role, the debate might have settled on the wrong year due to lack of specific knowledge.
